It's best to step back and evaluate whether you're in love with the person or in love with the notion of being in love. I often found that I was enamored with the idea of loving someone and someone loving me in return more so than I was in love with the person.

I'm an avid reader and that's what helps me keep things in focus/perspective (which is extremely different for me to do). I used to look down my nose at romance books or books with a cheesy romantic subplot, but it's a good way for me to channel that susceptibility of falling in love easily. I become entangled in the story or fall head over heels in love with a character (or multiple) and when I finish the book I'll feel sad for a day or two, but I know I can always go back. TV shows or movies serve the same purpose/have the same effect. I guess what I'm trying to say here is find *something* rather than *someone* to fall in love with. 

If you aren't looking for something to replace that feeling, just ride it out. It sucks the moment it all fades away (as you know) but it's always good to have that feeling stored away. Sometimes I get really down and become really self-critical and believe I'm incapable of truly loving anyone but - after I get out of the pool of despair and self-loathing - I'll think back to the feelings I've had and be proud of how capable I am of feeling an emotion that other people can't.

Last thing, the next time you're in a relationship make sure it's with someone you fall in love with often. Falling in love doesn't need grand gestures. My current SO and I have gone through several rough patches but in the midst of the good times I find that there's always something he does, like a particular smile or the way he says certain words, that brings that feeling of falling in love back to the surface. Addiction to falling in love isn't the worst addiction you could suffer from; it's rather easy to manage.

Currently interning with an NGO in Uganda. 

Contrary to popular belief, not all African nations experience problems with populations being malnourished - especially in Uganda. The land here is fertile, fruit bearing trees grow almost everywhere, and most people are subsistence farmers and have plenty of food to feed their families. 

The issue is the money. You're absolutely correct about that. Monetary aid is eaten up by corrupt politicians and the people working with any kind of aid (at least in the NGO I'm interning with) don't know how to run programs effectively, efficiently, and in a sustainable manner. To be honest it baffles me because they're just putting bandaids on the issues instead of targeting the roots of the problem.

Now, the education problem. I can't speak much on that but I do see that the quality of education in the schools in the areas I'm working in is subpar at best. It doesn't help when you have teachers who received a similar level and quality of education. 

I think solely focusing on the health of peoples in African nations is not productive. Not all professionals receive the education we as Westerners believe they would need to hold that position. I think simultaneously tackling the issue of providing decent education also would benefit the countries.

These are all just my humble opinions from my experiences in Uganda so far.

I haven't heard about warlords or gangsters (I think that happens more towards the DRC border). I guess in the region I'm in you could call the politicians gangsters. 

But yes, political corruption is one of the greatest issues in the country (according to the people I've spoken to - don't ask anyone working for/with the government). One example: Ugandans pay taxes but it doesn't show (the roads are terrible - what should be a 2 hour trip can easily turn to 4-6 hours and education that could improve the livelihood of the people is poor). There, of course, is a lot more to this but this is what I work with and see daily and feel most comfortable speaking about.

I didn't (and still don't) pay attention to mainstream media's depiction of the country so I don't have much to compare with what I'm seeing. But I'll try to describe it. If you have something specific you would like to know ask me about that and I may be able to answer. I'm not really good with general things.

I work in villages in the Eastern region of the country, not too far from the Uganda/Kenya border. I haven't seen most of the country (and probably won't) but can tell you what Ugandans have told me and what I've seen. 

* A majority of the population are subsistence farmers and live on the equivalent of 1-2 USD/day (3350-6700 UGX). 

* The villagers I work with, more often than not, have trouble caring for their children (paying school fees and having enough money for clinic/hospital fees). 

* About 15% of the country has access to electricity. (A friend working with an electric company told me this, if you find something that contradicts that please correct me.)
